title: Design and Implement an LRU Cache
prompt: Design a data structure for a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. It supports get(key) and put(key, value). get returns the value if the key exists, else -1, and marks the key as most-recently used. put inserts or updates the value; if the cache exceeds its fixed capacity, it evicts the least-recently-used key. Both operations must run in O(1) average time.
blurb: The classic O(1) cache design — a hash map for lookup plus a doubly linked list for recency ordering.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Restates the O(1) requirement for both get and put, and that both operations touch recency, not just get.

rubric.label: Approach & data-structure choice
rubric.description: Reaches hashmap + doubly linked list; explains why a singly linked list or array can't hit O(1) eviction/reordering.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: put on an existing key updates value AND moves to front; eviction removes the true LRU node and its map entry; get reorders.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: States O(1) time for get/put and O(capacity) space, and justifies why the DLL gives O(1) splice.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean node struct, sentinel head/tail dummies to avoid null checks, small helper methods (remove/addFront), no duplicated pointer surgery.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Capacity 1, updating an existing key at capacity (no eviction), get on missing key, put then get same key.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Walks a sequence of ops verifying eviction order and reordering; checks the dummy-node boundaries.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Narrates the pointer manipulation clearly and keeps the map and list in sync in the explanation.

constraints: Up to ~2*10^5 calls to get and put combined
get and put must each be O(1) average time

examples.input: LRUCache(2); put(1,1); put(2,2); get(1); put(3,3); get(2); put(4,4); get(1); get(3); get(4)
examples.explanation: Capacity 2. put(3,3) evicts key 2 (LRU, since get(1) had just touched 1). Later put(4,4) evicts key 1 because get(3) had made 3 more-recent than 1.

test_cases.expected: get(2)=2 then -1 — 2 evicted after 1 and 4 inserted

approaches.name: brute force (array/list + linear scan)
approaches.idea: Store entries in a list; on get, scan for the key and move it to the end; on put over capacity, pop the front. Simple but every access is a linear scan and every reorder shifts elements.

approaches.name: ordered map / language builtin
approaches.idea: Use an insertion-ordered map (e.g. Java LinkedHashMap with accessOrder, Python OrderedDict move_to_end/popitem). Correct and concise but hides the mechanism the interviewer wants to see.

approaches.name: optimal: hashmap + doubly linked list
approaches.idea: HashMap maps key -> node. A doubly linked list orders nodes by recency, most-recent at the front (next to a dummy head), least-recent at the back (next to a dummy tail). get: look up node, unlink it, re-insert at front, return value. put: if present, update value and move to front; else create node, insert at front, add to map, and if size > capacity remove the tail's predecessor and delete it from the map. Dummy head/tail sentinels remove null-boundary special cases.

follow_ups: Make it thread-safe for concurrent get/put. Discuss a single mutex vs. sharding the cache into striped segments each with its own lock and DLL.
Extend to an LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache — how does the structure change? (frequency buckets, each a DLL, plus a min-frequency pointer for O(1)).
Add per-entry TTL / expiry — lazy expiry on access vs. a background sweeper, and interaction with LRU eviction.
Support O(1) getRandomKey or approximate LRU (sampling, as Redis does) to save memory on the pointers.
Generic key/value types and a size-based (bytes) rather than count-based capacity.
reference.reference_solution: Maintain: map[key]->Node and a doubly linked list with dummy head and dummy tail. Node holds {key, value, prev, next}. Helpers: remove(node) splices node out (node.prev.next=node.next; node.next.prev=node.prev); addFront(node) inserts just after head (node.next=head.next; node.prev=head; head.next.prev=node; head.next=node). get(key): if key not in map return -1; node=map[key]; remove(node); addFront(node); return node.value. put(key,value): if key in map: node=map[key]; node.value=value; remove(node); addFront(node); return. Else create node; map[key]=node; addFront(node); if len(map) > capacity: lru = tail.prev; remove(lru); delete map[lru.key]. Storing key on the node is essential so eviction can delete the correct map entry. Every operation is a constant number of pointer swaps plus O(1) map ops.
pitfalls: Forgetting to store the key inside the node — then you can't delete the evicted entry from the map in O(1).
On put of an existing key at capacity, evicting anyway (it's an update, not an insert).
Moving to front on put-update but not on get, or vice versa.
Omitting dummy head/tail and drowning in null checks for first/last node.

interviewer_notes: Give the plain definition and let the candidate propose a structure. If they jump to a language builtin (OrderedDict/LinkedHashMap), acknowledge it's correct then ask them to implement the underlying structure — that's the real signal. Stay silent while they wire the pointers; only nudge if they stall for a while, and the best nudge is 'what breaks with a singly linked list?' which leads them to needing prev pointers for O(1) removal. Watch specifically for: storing key-in-node for eviction, and moving-to-front on BOTH get and put-update. If they get a clean working version quickly, escalate to the thread-safety follow-up (single lock vs. striped locks) and, for a strong senior signal, LFU.
